title: Impacts of Illuminance and Correlated Color Temperature on Cognitive Performance: A VR-Lighting Study
research_question: How do different lighting conditions (illuminance and CCT) influence auditory memory scores (RQ1a), visual memory scores (RQ1b), auditory memory response time (RQ2a), and visual memory response time (RQ2b)? Do architectural context (RQ1c, RQ2c) and experiment time (RQ1d, RQ2d) moderate these influences?

participants.description: Thirty-five healthy adult participants (M=26.51, SD=4.31, range 19-38 years). Majority were students and researchers (n=24), with engineers (n=4) and programmers (n=3). 19 male, 15 female, 1 non-binary. Around half (48.5%) used eyeglasses or contact lenses. All reported sufficient sleep and no medical problems. Most associated with Vienna University of Technology.
participants.recruitment: convenience sampling method (word-of-mouth and announcements through the university transmission system)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two distinct architectural contexts (modern interior classroom and meeting room) with identical dimensions (7m x 8m x 3m). Furniture and layout varied to convey room function. Five different artificial lighting conditions were simulated in each context, ranging from 600 lm to 4200 lm luminous flux and 2000 K to 7200 K CCT. These conditions corresponded to average illuminance levels of 100 lx, 400 lx, and 700 lx on the work plane. The conditions were: Warm-Dark (2000 K-600 lm/100 lx), Cold-Dark (7200 K-600 lm/100 lx), Neutral-Moderate (4600 K-2400 lm/400 lx), Warm-Bright (2000 K-4200 lm/700 lx), and Cold-Bright (7200 K-4200 lm/700 lx). The VR environment was developed in Unreal Engine 4.26 and presented via Meta Quest 2 head-mounted display.

mechanisms: Well-lit environments lead to faster and more accurate visual processing by triggering rapid chemical reactions in the retina, facilitating swift responses to stimuli.
Exposure to bright light or changes in lighting conditions can affect circadian rhythms and alter physiological state, impacting reaction time.
Poorly lit settings with reduced visibility and increased visual noise can slow reaction times by causing details to be overlooked and delaying visual information processing.
Motor responses and cognition depend on the integration of visual information and cognitive processing, which is influenced by light quality and availability.
Higher contrast ratio in the Visual Memory Task (VMT) is assumed to cause improved VMT scores under bright and dark conditions compared to moderate lighting.
implementation_implications: Architects and engineers should develop lighting designs sensitive to occupants' cognitive performance.
Lighting systems can be developed to promote better cognitive function and overall wellbeing.
Further research on lighting in educational spaces should focus on daytime contribution and task type during exposure to specific light conditions.
Evidence-based design methods using VR can become more affordable and accessible for pre-construction testing, analyzing user responses to lighting factors.
Lighting settings can be tailored for specific space use during the daytime based on user cognitive performance knowledge.
Results can be integrated with physiological measurements for a comprehensive understanding.
Combining VR with lighting offers possibilities for research with fully customizable environments and user interactions.

limitations: Measurements utilized in the study have yet to be validated against real-world measurement methods and should not be directly applied in real environments.
The potential limitations of the VR simulation could be a minor concern, requiring further research for validation in real-world environments.
The participant pool consisted mainly of university students (convenience sampling), limiting generalizability to a broader population.

The age distribution (young adults) and proportion of participants wearing eyeglasses might differ from the general population, potentially leading to different effects of lighting on task performance.
VR, while offering control, limits the number of participants tested at once, making broad conclusions challenging.
Data collection was constrained by geographical location, suggesting replication in different countries.
The experiment used relatively low-difficulty tasks, and future studies will involve more difficult trials.
